A financial services company runs a trading platform in `us-east4` and connects to its New York data center using two Dedicated Interconnect connections in the same metropolitan area, each in a different edge availability domain. A new regulatory requirement mandates that the hybrid connection be designed to meet Google's highest published availability SLA. The on-premises team can extend circuits to a second colocation facility in another metro. What should the network engineer implement?
Add two more Dedicated Interconnect connections in the same metro, placing all four in alternating edge availability domains, with a single Cloud Router.
Keep the existing topology and add an HA VPN gateway as a backup path over the internet.

Provision four Dedicated Interconnect connections—two in each of two metros, each pair spanning both edge availability domains—use Cloud Routers in two regions, and set the VPC dynamic routing mode to global.
Replace Dedicated Interconnect with Partner Interconnect in two metros using Layer 3 partners.

Google's 99.99% Interconnect topology requires at least four connections across two metros (two edge availability domains per metro), Cloud Routers in two regions, and global dynamic routing so every region can use every path.

Two connections in one metro, regardless of how many are added there, cap out at the 99.9% topology; an HA VPN backup does not change the Interconnect SLA tier, and switching to Partner Interconnect adds provider dependency without being required.

The security team requires that data can never be copied to a Cloud Storage bucket or BigQuery dataset outside the company's organization, even with valid stolen credentials. Traffic must not traverse the public internet. Which design meets these requirements?

Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the data projects, configure on-premises DNS to resolve `*.googleapis.com` to `restricted.googleapis.com`, and advertise `199.36.153.4/30` to on-premises using Cloud Router custom route advertisements.
Configure on-premises DNS to resolve `*.googleapis.com` to `private.googleapis.com` and advertise `199.36.153.8/30` through Cloud Router, with IAM deny policies on external buckets.
Create egress VPC firewall rules that allow only the Google API IP ranges and deny all other destinations.
Place Cloud Armor security policies in front of BigQuery and Cloud Storage to restrict which identities can call the APIs.

VPC Service Controls blocks data movement across the perimeter boundary even with valid credentials, and the `restricted.googleapis.com` VIP (`199.36.153.4/30`) only serves VPC-SC-supported APIs so traffic is forced through perimeter enforcement privately over Interconnect.

The `private.googleapis.com` VIP provides private access but does not enforce the perimeter; firewall rules cannot distinguish buckets owned by different organizations because they share the same API endpoints, and Cloud Armor does not front Google APIs.

A DNS forwarding zone for `example.com` pointing to an on-premises resolver that returns the internal address.
A DNS response policy rule on the public zone that returns the internal IP for all clients.
A single public zone with two A records for `shop.example.com`, one public and one internal.
A private managed zone for `example.com` authorized for the production VPC containing an A record for `shop` pointing to the internal load balancer, alongside the existing public zone.

Two records in one public zone would return the internal IP to internet users as well, a response policy applies to VPC queries rather than creating a dual view, and forwarding to on-premises adds an unnecessary dependency.

Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider, with VLAN attachments sized for the required bandwidth.
HA VPN with four tunnels aggregated using ECMP.
Direct Peering through an internet exchange point.
Partner Interconnect is designed for customers who cannot reach a Google colocation facility, with attachment capacities up to 50 Gbps and SLA-backed topologies.
Dedicated Interconnect requires meeting Google in a colocation facility, HA VPN runs over the internet with per-tunnel throughput limits, and Direct Peering doesn't provide private VPC access.

A company's Dedicated Interconnect VLAN attachments and Cloud Router are in `us-east4`. New subnets were created in `us-west1` and `europe-west1`, but on-premises routers only learn `us-east4` subnet routes, and on-premises traffic cannot reach the new regions. What is the most likely fix?
Change the VPC's dynamic routing mode from regional to global.

Add static routes on-premises pointing to the new subnets via the Interconnect.
Enable Private Google Access on the new subnets.

In regional dynamic routing mode, a Cloud Router only advertises subnets and applies learned routes in its own region; global mode makes subnets in all regions advertised and learned routes usable everywhere.

A retail chain has 300 stores using a third-party SD-WAN solution. It wants the stores to reach workloads in multiple VPCs and to use Google's backbone for store-to-store traffic between regions. The SD-WAN appliances can run as VMs in Google Cloud and speak BGP. What should the engineer design?
One HA VPN tunnel per store terminated on Cloud VPN gateways.
Direct Peering from each regional SD-WAN hub.
SD-WAN virtual appliances in Google Cloud registered as router appliance spokes on a Network Connectivity Center hub, peering with Cloud Router via BGP.

A company is planning a hybrid environment spanning on-premises (`10.0.0.0/12`), AWS (`172.16.0.0/16`), and Google Cloud. It expects future acquisitions. What is the best practice for Google Cloud address planning?
Use auto mode VPCs so ranges are chosen automatically.
Allocate a documented, non-overlapping supernet for Google Cloud from a central IP address management plan, and reserve space for growth, GKE secondary ranges, and PSA ranges.
Reuse `10.0.0.0/12` in Google Cloud and rely on Cloud NAT for translation.
Use `172.16.0.0/16` in Google Cloud since AWS traffic will be routed separately.

A centralized IPAM plan with a dedicated non-overlapping supernet, including room for GKE secondary ranges and Private Service Access allocations, prevents routing conflicts across hybrid and multicloud networks.

A company created a Cloud DNS outbound forwarding zone for `corp.example.com` targeting on-premises DNS servers at `10.1.1.53` and `10.1.1.54`. The HA VPN tunnels are up, and VMs can ping the DNS servers, but DNS queries from VMs for `corp.example.com` time out. What is the most likely cause?
Private Google Access is disabled on the VM subnets.
The forwarding zone must use public IP targets.
On-premises routers have no route back to Cloud DNS's source range `35.199.192.0/19`, which must be advertised from Cloud Router as a custom route.
Cloud DNS forwarding requires Cloud NAT to reach on-premises servers.
Forwarded queries to private targets originate from `35.199.192.0/19`, so on-premises networks need a route for that range back through the VPN, typically via a Cloud Router custom advertisement.
Private Google Access and Cloud NAT are unrelated to forwarding, and forwarding zones support private RFC 1918 targets.

On-premises applications must resolve records in Cloud DNS private zones authorized for `prod-vpc`, which connects to on-premises via Cloud Interconnect. What should the engineer configure?
Create an inbound DNS server policy on `prod-vpc` and configure on-premises DNS servers to conditionally forward the private zones to the inbound forwarder IP addresses.
Create an outbound forwarding zone for the private zones pointing to on-premises DNS.
Make the zones public and restrict access with firewall rules.
Create a DNS peering zone from on-premises to `prod-vpc`.
An inbound server policy creates entry-point IPs in the VPC's subnets that on-premises resolvers can forward to over hybrid connectivity to resolve private zones.
Outbound forwarding goes the other direction, public zones expose internal records, and DNS peering only works between VPC networks.

A company has a `dns-hub` VPC with Interconnect to on-premises and outbound forwarding zones for `corp.example.com`. Fifteen workload VPCs, not peered with `dns-hub` and not connected to on-premises, must resolve `corp.example.com` through the same path. What is the most scalable design?
Duplicate outbound forwarding zones in each workload VPC.
Deploy BIND servers in each workload VPC.
Configure an inbound server policy in each workload VPC.
Create DNS peering zones in each workload VPC targeting `dns-hub` for `corp.example.com`.
DNS peering lets a VPC send queries for a zone to another VPC's resolution order, so the hub's forwarding zones serve every workload VPC without network connectivity to on-premises.
Duplicated forwarding zones in unconnected VPCs cannot reach on-premises servers, self-managed BIND adds operational overhead, and inbound policies handle queries entering from outside.

A payment processor uses Partner Interconnect. A new PCI DSS interpretation requires all traffic between the data center and Google Cloud to be encrypted with IPsec. The company wants to keep the Interconnect's private bandwidth. What should the engineer implement?
Enable MACsec on the Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments.
Deploy HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect using encrypted VLAN attachments.
Replace Partner Interconnect with HA VPN over the internet.
Enable TLS on every application and keep the Interconnect unencrypted.
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect runs IPsec tunnels across encrypted VLAN attachments, keeping private connectivity while satisfying an IPsec requirement.

A company wants to improve internet performance to Google Cloud services for branch offices but cannot justify Direct Peering or Interconnect. Its regional ISP is listed in Google's Verified Peering Provider program. What does using this ISP provide?
Private RFC 1918 access to VPC resources through the ISP.
An SLA-backed 99.99% dedicated connection to Google Cloud.
Well-connected, redundant internet paths to Google's edge for reaching Google public services, without the company peering directly with Google.
Automatic encryption of all traffic to Google APIs.
Verified Peering Providers are ISPs that meet Google's peering and redundancy criteria, improving access to Google's public services over the internet.

A company connects Google Cloud to Microsoft Azure using HA VPN. The Azure VPN gateway is active-active with two public IPs. The company wants Google's 99.99% HA VPN SLA. How should the connection be configured?
An HA VPN gateway with an external (peer) VPN gateway resource defining two interfaces, four tunnels (each HA VPN interface to each Azure IP), and BGP sessions on each tunnel.
A Classic VPN gateway with two tunnels to the two Azure IPs.
An HA VPN gateway with one tunnel to one Azure IP and a static route backup.
Cross-Cloud Interconnect with a single VLAN attachment.

For a peer with two interfaces, Google's recommended HA VPN topology uses a two-interface external VPN gateway and four tunnels with BGP to achieve the 99.99% SLA. Classic VPN is limited to 99.9%, a single tunnel doesn't qualify for 99.99%, and a single VLAN attachment lacks redundancy.

A company is creating a GKE Standard cluster with the default maximum of 110 Pods per node and expects to scale to 500 nodes. What is the smallest Pod secondary range that supports this scale?
With 110 max Pods per node, GKE assigns each node a `/24` (256 addresses), so 500 nodes need 128,000 addresses; a `/15` provides 131,072.
A `/16` supports only 256 nodes, a `/17` supports 128, and a `/14` works but wastes address space.

A platform team runs lightweight workloads with at most 30 Pods per node, so it sets the cluster's maximum Pods per node to 32. It plans for up to 1,000 nodes. What Pod secondary range should it allocate?
GKE allocates a per-node block twice the maximum Pods rounded up to a power of two, so 32 max Pods yields a `/26` (64 addresses); 1,000 nodes × 64 = 64,000 addresses, which fits in a `/16` (65,536).
A `/18` supports 256 nodes, a `/20` only 64, and a `/14` is four times more than needed.

A production GKE cluster has exhausted its Pod secondary range, so new nodes fail to be created. The cluster must keep running, and the existing range cannot be expanded because adjacent space is used. What should the engineer do?
Recreate the cluster with a larger Pod range and migrate workloads.
Change the cluster's Service range to a larger block.
Add a new secondary range to the subnet and create a new node pool that uses it as an additional Pod range.
Increase maximum Pods per node on the existing node pools.
GKE supports discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR, allowing new node pools to use additional Pod ranges without recreating the cluster.
Recreating the cluster is disruptive, the Service range doesn't provide Pod addresses, and raising max Pods per node increases per-node block size and consumes the range faster.

When planning a GKE cluster's Service (ClusterIP) range in a VPC-native cluster connected to on-premises, which statement is correct?
The Service range should not overlap with any subnet, secondary range, or on-premises/peered range, even though ClusterIPs are only used within the cluster.
The Service range can overlap on-premises ranges because ClusterIPs are never routed outside the cluster.
The Service range must be a public range to support external load balancers.
The Service range is automatically expanded when it's exhausted.
Best practice is to allocate the Service range from non-overlapping space so traffic to on-premises or peered destinations in that range isn't intercepted by cluster Service routing.

A security team requires that GKE nodes have no external IP addresses, and that the Kubernetes control plane be reachable only from the corporate office's public egress range `203.0.113.0/24` and from the VPC. Developers use kubectl from the office. What should the engineer configure?
Public nodes with a firewall rule restricting SSH to `203.0.113.0/24`.
Private nodes with the control plane's public endpoint disabled.
Private nodes with no authorized networks configured.
Private nodes with the public endpoint enabled and authorized networks limited to `203.0.113.0/24`.
Private nodes remove external IPs, and authorized networks restrict public-endpoint access to the office range while VPC access uses the private endpoint.

A service project team wants to create a GKE cluster in a Shared VPC subnet owned by the host project. Cluster creation fails with permission errors on the subnet. Secondary ranges for Pods and Services already exist on the subnet. What must be granted?
`roles/container.admin` on the host project to the service project's developers.

`roles/compute.networkUser` on the subnet to the service project's GKE service agent and Google APIs service agent, and `roles/container.hostServiceAgentUser` on the host project to the GKE service agent.
`roles/compute.xpnAdmin` to the service project's GKE service agent.
`roles/owner` on the host project to the service project's Compute Engine default service account.

GKE in Shared VPC requires the service project's GKE and Google APIs service agents to have Network User on the subnet, and the GKE service agent needs Host Service Agent User on the host project to manage firewall resources.
The other options grant broad or unrelated roles and violate least privilege.

A company is migrating to GKE Autopilot and asks whether it can install Calico to enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, as it did on self-managed clusters. What should the engineer tell them?
Autopilot supports Calico when enabled at cluster creation.
Autopilot doesn't support NetworkPolicy; use firewall rules instead.
Autopilot uses GKE Dataplane V2, which enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy natively, so Calico isn't needed or supported.
Autopilot requires Istio sidecars to enforce NetworkPolicy.

Autopilot clusters use GKE Dataplane V2 (eBPF-based), which enforces NetworkPolicy natively, and users can't install their own CNI. NetworkPolicy is supported, VPC firewall rules don't provide Pod-level policy, and a service mesh isn't required.

A `/22` has 1,024 addresses, and after Google reserves four per subnet, 1,020 are usable for nodes.
A `/23` has 508 usable addresses and a `/24` has 252, while a `/21` works but is larger than needed.

Pods in a VPC-native GKE cluster must connect to an on-premises database at `10.200.5.20` over Cloud Interconnect. The on-premises firewall only allows the node subnet range, not the Pod range, and security won't change it. Connections from Pods are dropped. What should the engineer do?
Configure Cloud NAT for the Pod range.
Advertise the Pod range to on-premises via Cloud Router.
Recreate the cluster as a routes-based cluster.
Configure the ip-masq-agent so the on-premises range is not in `nonMasqueradeCIDRs`, causing Pod traffic to on-premises to be SNATed to the node IP.

By default, GKE doesn't masquerade traffic to RFC 1918 destinations, so on-premises sees Pod IPs; customizing ip-masq-agent to exclude the on-premises range makes that traffic use the node IP the firewall allows.
Public Cloud NAT handles internet egress, advertising Pod ranges doesn't satisfy the firewall constraint, and routes-based clusters are legacy and still use Pod IPs.

Administrators need to run kubectl from on-premises against a GKE cluster whose control plane has only a private endpoint enabled. The on-premises network connects to the cluster's VPC via HA VPN. Commands time out. What should the engineer do?
Enable the public endpoint without authorized networks.

Add the on-premises range to the cluster's authorized networks, and ensure the control-plane endpoint's range is advertised to on-premises through Cloud Router (for peering-based control planes, export custom routes on the GKE peering).
Create a Cloud NAT gateway for the control-plane range.
Enable Private Google Access on the node subnet.

Reaching a private control-plane endpoint from on-premises requires authorized networks to include the on-premises range and a routable path, which means advertising the endpoint range and, for peering-based control planes, exporting routes so return traffic works.
Enabling an open public endpoint weakens security, Cloud NAT doesn't provide inbound reachability, and Private Google Access doesn't reach the control plane.

A data engineering team runs Dataproc clusters on VMs without external IP addresses. Clusters in `subnet-a` can read from Cloud Storage, but identical clusters in `subnet-b` of the same VPC and region fail with connection timeouts to `storage.googleapis.com`. Both subnets use the same firewall rules and the VPC still has its default internet gateway route. What is the most likely fix?
Assign external IP addresses to the VMs in `subnet-b`.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway for `subnet-b` only.
Create a VPC Network Peering connection to `servicenetworking.googleapis.com`.
Private Google Access is configured per subnet, and it lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs through the default internet gateway route.

External IPs or Cloud NAT would also work but add public exposure or cost that isn't required, and the `servicenetworking` peering is for Private Service Access to managed services like Cloud SQL, not Google APIs.

To prevent any direct internet egress, a security team deleted the `0.0.0.0/0` default internet gateway route from a production VPC. Private Google Access remains enabled on all subnets, but workloads can no longer reach Cloud Storage or BigQuery. The team wants API access restored without re-enabling general internet egress. What should the engineer do?
Create DNS records mapping `*.googleapis.com` to `private.googleapis.com` and a custom static route for `199.36.153.8/30` with next hop `default-internet-gateway`.
Re-create the `0.0.0.0/0` route with priority 65535 so it's used only as a last resort.
Deploy Cloud NAT and restrict it to Google API ranges.
Disable and re-enable Private Google Access on each subnet to refresh routing.

Private Google Access still requires a route to Google API addresses via the default internet gateway, so pointing DNS at the `private.googleapis.com` VIP and adding a route for only `199.36.153.8/30` restores API access without a general internet path.
A low-priority default route still provides internet egress, Cloud NAT can't filter by destination, and toggling the setting doesn't create the missing route.

A network engineer has the Owner role on both a new network project and three application projects. When the engineer tries to enable the network project as a Shared VPC host project, the operation fails with a permission error. What does the engineer need?
The `roles/compute.networkAdmin` role on the network project.
The Organization Administrator role on the organization.
The `roles/compute.networkUser` role on each application project.
The Shared VPC Admin role (`roles/compute.xpnAdmin`) at the organization or folder level.
Enabling a host project and attaching service projects requires the Shared VPC Admin role granted at the organization or folder level containing the projects.

Project Owner and Network Admin are project-scoped and don't include Shared VPC administration, Network User is for consuming subnets, and Organization Administrator manages IAM but isn't itself the Shared VPC permission.

A company adopts Shared VPC. The finance team asks where costs for VMs in service projects will be billed, and the security team asks where firewall rules protecting those VMs will be created and managed. What is the correct answer?
VM costs are billed to the host project; firewall rules are created in each service project.
VM costs are billed to the service project; firewall rules for the Shared VPC network are created in the host project.
VM costs and firewall rules are both in the host project.
VM costs and firewall rules are both in the service project.
Resources such as VMs belong to and are billed to the service project in which they are created, while the network itself, including its firewall rules and routes, lives in the host project.
This separation lets application teams own costs while the network team retains control of network policy.

`vpc-a` and `vpc-b` are peered, and `vpc-a` exports custom routes while `vpc-b` imports them. In `vpc-a`, a static route for `172.20.0.0/16` points to a NAT VM and applies only to VMs with the network tag `legacy`. Engineers notice the route never appears in `vpc-b`. What is the reason?
Static routes are never exported over VPC Network Peering.
Custom route import requires global dynamic routing on `vpc-b`.
Static routes that use network tags are not exchanged over VPC Network Peering.
The route's destination overlaps a subnet in `vpc-b`.
Custom static routes can be exchanged over peering when export and import are enabled, but routes scoped with network tags are never exchanged.
Dynamic routing mode affects Cloud Router routes rather than peering import, and an overlap would produce a different error or conflict than a silently missing tagged route.

`vpc-a` uses a subnet with a privately used public IPv4 (PUPI) range, `52.10.0.0/20`, for batch VMs. `vpc-a` is peered with `vpc-b`, and all other subnets are reachable from `vpc-b`, but the PUPI subnet is not present in `vpc-b`'s routing table. What should the engineer configure?
Enable importing subnet routes with public IPs on `vpc-b`'s side of the peering.
Enable custom route export on `vpc-a` and custom route import on `vpc-b`.
Create a static route in `vpc-b` for `52.10.0.0/20` with the peering as the next hop.
Re-create the subnet using an RFC 1918 range; PUPI subnets cannot be peered.
By default, a network exports its PUPI subnet routes, but the peer does not import them until import of subnet routes with public IPs is enabled on its side.
Custom route settings apply to static and dynamic routes rather than subnet routes, peering can't be a static route next hop, and PUPI subnets can be peered.

A team created a new custom-mode VPC and deployed VMs with no external IPs. Admins must SSH using Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding. The IAM `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` role is granted, but connections fail. No firewall rules exist yet. What should the engineer add?
An egress rule allowing TCP 22 to `0.0.0.0/0`.
An ingress rule allowing TCP 22 from `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22`.
A Cloud NAT gateway so IAP can reach the VMs.
An ingress rule allowing TCP 22 from `35.235.240.0/20` to the target VMs.

Custom-mode VPCs have only the implied deny-ingress rule, so an ingress rule must allow TCP 22 from IAP's forwarding range `35.235.240.0/20`. Egress is already allowed by the implied rule, the other ranges are for load balancer health checks, and Cloud NAT only handles outbound traffic.

A company uses Private Service Access for Cloud SQL and Memorystore with an allocated range of `10.100.0.0/24`. Creating new Cloud SQL instances in another region now fails with an error indicating insufficient IP space in the allocated range. What should the engineer do?
Expand the allocated range to `/20` using the subnet expand command.
Allocate an additional IP range for Private Service Access and update the private services connection to include both the existing and new ranges.
Delete the private connection and recreate it with a larger range.
Create the new instances with public IP only.
You can add allocated ranges to an existing private services connection by updating it with the full list of ranges, without disrupting existing instances.
Allocated ranges aren't subnets and can't be expanded with the subnet command, deleting the connection disrupts existing services, and public IP contradicts the private design.

An engineer is deploying a regional internal Application Load Balancer in `us-central1` to front microservices in a Shared VPC. Creating the forwarding rule fails with an error indicating that a required subnet is missing. What must be created?
A second subnet with Private Google Access enabled.
A Private Service Connect subnet in the region.
A proxy-only subnet in `us-central1` with purpose `REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY` and role `ACTIVE`.
A subnet with a secondary range reserved for load balancer VIPs.
Envoy-based regional load balancers, including the internal Application Load Balancer, require a proxy-only subnet in the region and VPC from which the proxies source traffic to backends.
Private Google Access isn't related, PSC subnets are for producer NAT, and VIPs come from a regular subnet rather than a secondary range.

A VPC has a dynamic route for `10.0.0.0/8` learned from on-premises through Cloud Router with priority 100, and a custom static route for `10.1.0.0/16` pointing to a firewall appliance with priority 1000. A VM sends a packet to `10.1.5.20`. Which route is used?
The static route for `10.1.0.0/16`, because Google Cloud selects the most specific destination before considering priority.
The dynamic route for `10.0.0.0/8`, because it has the lower priority value.
The dynamic route, because dynamic routes always take precedence over static routes.
Google Cloud route selection first chooses the longest prefix match, and priority only breaks ties between routes with the same destination prefix.
ECMP applies only to equal prefixes and priorities, and dynamic routes don't automatically take precedence over static routes.

A company operates three self-managed NAT VMs for a legacy application that requires specific source IPs. The engineer wants outbound traffic from tagged application VMs to be distributed across all three NAT VMs. How should the routes be configured?
Three static routes for `0.0.0.0/0` with priorities 800, 900, and 1000, each pointing to one NAT VM.
Three static routes for `0.0.0.0/0` with the same priority and the same network tag, each with a different NAT VM as next-hop instance.
One static route pointing to a managed instance group of NAT VMs.
A policy-based route with three next hops.
When multiple routes share the same destination and priority, Google Cloud uses equal-cost multipath (ECMP) to spread flows across the next hops.
Different priorities create active/standby behavior rather than distribution, an instance group isn't a valid static route next hop, and policy-based routes take a single next hop.

A VPC in global dynamic routing mode has Cloud Routers in `us-east4` and `us-west1`, each receiving `192.168.0.0/16` from on-premises with the same MED over separate Interconnects. VMs in `us-west1` send traffic through the `us-west1` Interconnect, and VMs in `us-east4` use the `us-east4` Interconnect. Why?
Regional subnets can only use Cloud Routers in their own region.
The on-premises routers are sending different AS paths to each region.
Cloud Router always prefers the most recently learned route.
In global mode, routes learned in another region have an inter-region cost added to their priority, so the local region's route has a better priority.
With global dynamic routing, Google Cloud adds a region-to-region cost to the base priority of routes learned in other regions, so VMs prefer same-region paths when MEDs are equal.
In global mode, subnets can use Cloud Routers in any region, the scenario states identical advertisements, and Cloud Router doesn't prefer routes based on recency.

A company is migrating a legacy application whose VMs must send all internet traffic through an explicit proxy VM for compliance, while other VMs in the same subnet should continue using the default internet gateway. The legacy VMs are tagged `legacy-app`. What should the engineer configure?
A policy-based route matching the subnet's source range with the proxy VM as next hop.
Delete the default route and add a `0.0.0.0/0` route to the proxy VM for everyone.
A static route for `0.0.0.0/0` with next hop the proxy VM, network tag `legacy-app`, and priority 900.
A static route for `0.0.0.0/0` with next hop the proxy VM and priority 1100.
Tag-scoped static routes apply only to VMs with that tag, and priority 900 beats the default internet gateway route's priority of 1000 for those VMs.
A source-range policy-based route would capture every VM in the subnet, removing the default route affects all VMs, and priority 1100 loses to the default route.

An on-premises team begins advertising `0.0.0.0/0` to Google Cloud over Cloud Interconnect with a MED of 100. The VPC still has the default internet gateway route with priority 1000. What happens to internet-bound traffic from VMs?
It is sent to on-premises over the Interconnect, because the learned default route has a better priority than the default internet gateway route.
It continues to use the default internet gateway, because system-generated routes can't be overridden.
It is load-balanced between both routes using ECMP.
It is dropped, because two default routes conflict.
Both routes have the same prefix, so priority decides, and the learned route's priority of 100 beats the default route's 1000, forcing internet traffic on-premises.
The default internet gateway route is a custom-editable route, ECMP applies only to equal priorities, and conflicting routes are resolved by priority rather than dropped.

An engineer created a policy-based route that sends all traffic from `app-subnet` (`10.30.0.0/24`) to an internal passthrough load balancer fronting inspection appliances. Afterward, traffic between VMs within the VPC's own internal ranges (`10.0.0.0/8`) is also being sent through the appliances, adding latency. Internal traffic must bypass inspection. What should the engineer do?
Delete the policy-based route and use tagged static routes instead.
Lower the priority of the VPC's subnet routes.
Add firewall rules to deny traffic to the appliances from internal ranges.
Create a higher-priority policy-based route matching source `10.30.0.0/24` and destination `10.0.0.0/8` with next hop set to default routing.

Policy-based routes are evaluated before other routes, and a higher-priority PBR that sends matching traffic to default routing (`--next-hop-other-routes=DEFAULT_ROUTING`) makes internal flows bypass the appliance.
Tagged routes don't provide source-based steering for the whole subnet, subnet route priorities can't be changed, and firewall denies would break the traffic.

A company has 180 subnets within `10.20.0.0/16` in Google Cloud. The on-premises edge router has a limit on accepted prefixes and has begun rejecting routes. The network team wants on-premises to receive a single summary route. What should the engineer configure on Cloud Router?
Change the VPC to regional dynamic routing mode.
Configure custom advertisement mode, remove the "all subnets" advertisement, and advertise `10.20.0.0/16` as a custom IP range.
Enable BGP route aggregation on the VLAN attachments.
Custom advertisement mode lets Cloud Router advertise user-defined prefixes, such as a single summary, instead of every individual subnet.
Regional mode only limits which regions are advertised, VLAN attachments have no aggregation setting, and custom learned routes affect routes received into the VPC.

A partner's legacy router establishes a BGP session with Cloud Router but can't advertise the partner's `198.51.100.0/24` range due to a software limitation. The VPC must still route traffic for that range to the partner over this BGP session, and the route should be withdrawn automatically if the BGP session goes down. What should the engineer use?
A static route for `198.51.100.0/24` with the VLAN attachment as next hop.
A policy-based route for the destination with the Cloud Router as next hop.
Custom learned routes configured on the Cloud Router BGP peer for `198.51.100.0/24`.
A custom route advertisement for `198.51.100.0/24` on Cloud Router.
Custom learned routes make Cloud Router install routes as if they were received from the BGP peer, and those routes are withdrawn when the session goes down.
VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers aren't valid next hops for static or policy-based routes, and custom advertisements send routes to the peer rather than learning them.

To test an isolated environment, an engineer deletes the default internet gateway route from a VPC that hosts backends for a global external Application Load Balancer. The load balancer continues to serve traffic and health checks keep passing. Why?
Health check and Google Front End traffic uses special return paths that don't depend on the VPC's routes.
Deleting the default route only takes effect after VMs are restarted.
Load balancers create hidden `0.0.0.0/0` routes for their backends.
Health checks run from inside the VPC's subnets.
Google Cloud uses special routing paths for responses to health checkers and Google Front Ends, so these flows work without a default internet gateway route.

Route changes apply immediately, load balancers don't add hidden default routes, and health checks originate from Google ranges such as `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22` rather than from customer subnets.

A company has one shared-services VPC and 12 development VPCs, all non-overlapping. Every development VPC must reach the shared-services VPC, but development VPCs must never reach each other. The team wants a managed solution without writing firewall rules to block inter-dev traffic. What should the engineer configure?
An NCC hub using mesh topology with all VPCs as spokes.
VPC Network Peering from each dev VPC to the shared-services VPC, plus deny firewall rules.
Shared VPC with each dev team as a service project.
An NCC hub using star topology with the shared-services VPC in the center group and the development VPCs in the edge group.
NCC star topology lets edge spokes reach center spokes while preventing edge-to-edge connectivity, matching the isolation requirement without firewall rules.
Mesh topology connects all spokes, peering doesn't provide isolation on its own (it's non-transitive but needs a separate design for scale), and Shared VPC places everything in a single network.

A VPC that is an NCC VPC spoke contains a subnet `10.99.0.0/24` used for a sensitive management network. Other spokes must not learn routes to it, while the rest of the VPC's subnets must remain reachable. What should the engineer configure?
An egress deny firewall rule in each other spoke.
An export filter on the VPC spoke that excludes `10.99.0.0/24`.
Move the subnet to regional dynamic routing mode.
Remove the VPC from the hub and re-add it as a hybrid spoke.
VPC spokes support export filters (exclude or include ranges) that control which subnet routes are shared with the hub.
Firewall rules block traffic but still leak routes, dynamic routing mode doesn't apply to individual subnets, and hybrid spokes are for VPN, Interconnect, or router appliances.

A central networking team owns an NCC hub in the `net-hub` project. An application team adds its VPC, in a different project, as a VPC spoke. The spoke is created but remains inactive, and no routes are exchanged. What is required?
A hub administrator must review and accept the spoke proposal.
The application team must enable global dynamic routing on its VPC.
The spoke must be recreated in the `net-hub` project.
A Cloud Router must be created in the application VPC.
VPC spokes from a different project than the hub are created as proposals that the hub administrator must accept before they become active.
Dynamic routing mode and Cloud Routers aren't required for VPC spokes, and cross-project spokes are supported without moving resources.

A company connects offices in London and Singapore to Google Cloud with HA VPN tunnels in `europe-west2` and `asia-southeast1`. Both tunnel pairs are added as hybrid spokes to an NCC hub, but traffic between the two offices doesn't use Google's backbone—the offices still can't reach each other through Google Cloud. What is missing?
VPC Network Peering between the two regions.
A router appliance spoke in each region.
Site-to-site data transfer enabled on both hybrid spokes, in regions that support it.
Global dynamic routing mode on the hub.

For hybrid spokes to exchange routes and exchange traffic with each other across Google's network, site-to-site data transfer must be enabled on the spokes, and it's available only in supported regions.
Peering doesn't apply to on-premises sites, router appliances aren't required when using Cloud VPN, and the hub itself has no dynamic routing mode.

An engineer deploys a third-party SD-WAN virtual appliance in a VPC and registers it as an NCC router appliance spoke. BGP sessions come up, but traffic from branches destined for VMs in the VPC is dropped at the appliance, even though the appliance forwards packets correctly in its own logs. What configuration is most likely missing?
A Cloud NAT gateway for the appliance subnet.
Private Google Access on the appliance subnet.
A proxy-only subnet in the region.
IP forwarding (`canIpForward`) enabled on the router appliance VM.
Router appliance VMs send and receive packets whose source or destination isn't their own IP, which Google Cloud drops unless IP forwarding is enabled on the instance.
Cloud NAT, Private Google Access, and proxy-only subnets don't affect forwarding of transit traffic.

A company has 30 non-overlapping VPCs and a data center connected over Dedicated Interconnect in a `transit-vpc`. It has hit VPC Network Peering limits and wants every VPC and the data center to be able to reach each other through one managed construct. What should the engineer design?
Replace Interconnect with HA VPN in each VPC.
An NCC hub with the 30 VPCs as VPC spokes and the Interconnect VLAN attachments as hybrid spokes.
Shared VPC with all 30 VPCs merged into the transit VPC.
Cloud Router route advertisements from each VPC over peering.
NCC supports route exchange between VPC spokes and hybrid spokes, providing a scalable transit for both VPC-to-VPC and VPC-to-on-premises traffic without peering limits.
Per-VPC VPN is costly and duplicative, merging VPCs is a large redesign, and Cloud Routers don't advertise routes over peering.

Adding a newly acquired VPC as an NCC VPC spoke fails because its `172.16.8.0/24` subnet overlaps with a subnet in an existing spoke. That subnet in the new VPC hosts only a legacy tool that doesn't need to be reachable from other spokes. What is the fastest way to attach the VPC?
Configure the new spoke with an export exclusion filter for `172.16.8.0/24`.
Use VPC Network Peering instead of NCC for the new VPC.
Expand the existing spoke's subnet to absorb the overlapping range.
Enable Private Google Access on the overlapping subnet.
Excluding the overlapping range from the spoke's exported routes removes the conflict so the rest of the VPC can attach.
Peering also rejects overlapping subnets, expanding a subnet can't resolve overlap, and Private Google Access doesn't affect route exchange.

A GKE application behind an external Application Load Balancer created by an Ingress shows uneven load and extra latency. Traffic reaches nodes on a NodePort and is then forwarded by kube-proxy to Pods on other nodes. The team wants the load balancer to send traffic directly to Pods and health-check them individually. What should the engineer implement?
Change the Service type to `LoadBalancer` with `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`.
Deploy an Nginx ingress controller as a DaemonSet.
Use container-native load balancing with network endpoint groups (the `cloud.google.com/neg` annotation) on a VPC-native cluster.
Increase the number of nodes to spread the load.
Container-native load balancing uses zonal NEGs of Pod IPs so the load balancer targets and health-checks Pods directly, removing the extra node hop.
A `LoadBalancer` Service with `Cluster` policy still uses node-level forwarding, a self-managed ingress adds a proxy layer, and more nodes don't remove the double hop.

A platform team wants one global external load balancer shared by several application teams on a GKE cluster. The platform team must control the load balancer, certificates, and listeners, while each app team manages routing for its own hostnames in its own namespace. What should the engineer use?
One Ingress resource per namespace, each creating its own load balancer.
The GKE Gateway controller with a platform-owned `Gateway` (for example, class `gke-l7-global-external-managed`) and app-team-owned `HTTPRoute` resources in their namespaces.
A single Ingress resource in the platform namespace that the app teams edit.
A Service of type `LoadBalancer` per team with Cloud DNS weighted records.
The Gateway API separates roles: platform operators own the `Gateway` and its listeners, and app teams attach `HTTPRoute` resources from their own namespaces to a shared load balancer.
Per-namespace Ingresses create separate load balancers, a single shared Ingress breaks role separation, and `LoadBalancer` Services are L4 and don't share one L7 entry point.

A security team requires an audit trail of Kubernetes NetworkPolicy decisions, including which connections were allowed or denied between Pods, sent to Cloud Logging. The cluster is being created now. What should the engineer do?
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the node subnet.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on the GKE-managed firewall rules.
Deploy Calico with its flow-log add-on.
Create the cluster with GKE Dataplane V2 and enable network policy logging.
GKE Dataplane V2 supports network policy logging, which records allowed and denied connections evaluated by NetworkPolicy and exports them to Cloud Logging.
VPC Flow Logs and firewall logging don't show NetworkPolicy decisions, and Calico can't be combined with Dataplane V2's built-in enforcement.

In a GKE cluster with NetworkPolicy enforcement enabled, the `backend` namespace has a default-deny ingress policy. Pods labeled `app=api` in `backend` must accept TCP 8080 only from any Pod in the namespace labeled `team=frontend`. What NetworkPolicy should the engineer create in the `backend` namespace?
`podSelector: app=api` with an ingress rule `from: namespaceSelector: team=frontend` and port TCP 8080.
`podSelector: {}` with an ingress rule `from: podSelector: team=frontend` and port TCP 8080.
`podSelector: app=api` with an egress rule to `namespaceSelector: team=frontend` on TCP 8080.
A VPC firewall rule allowing TCP 8080 from the Pod range to the node range.
Selecting the `api` Pods and allowing ingress from a `namespaceSelector` matching the frontend namespace's label admits only those sources on port 8080.

A bare `podSelector` in `from` matches Pods in the same namespace and the empty selector opens all backend Pods, an egress rule controls the wrong direction, and VPC firewall rules don't enforce Pod-level namespace policy.
A compliance team uses VPC Flow Logs to monitor GKE traffic. They notice that communication between Pods running on the same node never appears in the logs. What should the engineer enable?
Increase the VPC Flow Logs sampling rate to 1.0.
Enable Packet Mirroring on the node subnet.
Enable intranode visibility on the cluster.
Enable metadata annotations on VPC Flow Logs.
Pod-to-Pod traffic on the same node doesn't leave the node, so VPC networking never sees it unless intranode visibility routes it through the VPC fabric.
Raising sampling or adding metadata can't log traffic that isn't observed, and Packet Mirroring has the same visibility gap.

A GKE cluster in `us-central1` exposes an internal Service using a `LoadBalancer` Service with the `networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"` annotation. Clients in `us-central1` connect successfully, but VMs in `us-east1` in the same VPC time out. What should the engineer do?
Create a firewall rule allowing traffic from `us-east1` subnets.
Add the `networking.gke.io/internal-load-balancer-allow-global-access: "true"` annotation to enable global access.
Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers only accept clients from the same region unless global access is enabled, which the annotation does for GKE Services.
NodePort doesn't solve regional access, firewall rules can't override the regional restriction, and dynamic routing mode affects Cloud Router routes.

A retailer runs identical GKE clusters in `us-east1` and `europe-west1`, both registered to a fleet. It wants one global anycast IP that routes users to the closest healthy cluster and automatically fails over if a cluster's Pods become unavailable. What should the engineer configure?
Two regional external Application Load Balancers with Cloud DNS geolocation routing.
Multi-cluster Gateway (or Multi Cluster Ingress) using a config cluster and the global external Application Load Balancer.
An external passthrough Network Load Balancer in each region.
Cloud Service Mesh with a single-cluster Ingress.
Multi-cluster Gateway and Multi Cluster Ingress program a global external Application Load Balancer across fleet clusters, giving one anycast IP with proximity routing and health-based failover.
DNS-based routing depends on TTLs and exposes multiple IPs, regional passthrough load balancers aren't global, and a single-cluster Ingress doesn't span clusters.

A fintech company's security team requires mutual TLS between all microservices across two GKE clusters, fine-grained authorization based on service identity, and traffic telemetry, without changing application code. What should the engineer implement?
Cloud Service Mesh with automatic sidecar injection (or managed data plane) and mTLS enforcement policies.
Cloud NGFW Enterprise with TLS inspection between Pods.
Internal Application Load Balancers in front of every service.
Cloud Service Mesh provides transparent mTLS, identity-based authorization policies, and telemetry for services without code changes, across clusters.

NetworkPolicy works at L3/L4 without encryption or service identity, NGFW inspects rather than provides service mTLS, and fronting each service with a load balancer doesn't give mutual authentication.

A private GKE cluster's nodes can reach the internet through Cloud NAT, but Pods can't reach external package repositories. The Cloud NAT gateway was configured by selecting the node subnet's primary IP range only. What should the engineer change?
Assign external IPs to the nodes.
Enable Private Google Access on the node subnet.
Update the Cloud NAT configuration to include the subnet's secondary (Pod) ranges, or all IP ranges of the subnet.
Configure ip-masq-agent to masquerade all traffic to node IPs, and remove Cloud NAT.
Pods in VPC-native clusters send egress traffic from Pod IPs in secondary ranges, so Cloud NAT must be configured for those ranges in addition to the primary range.
External IPs on nodes violate the private design, Private Google Access only covers Google APIs, and removing Cloud NAT would leave private nodes with no internet egress.

A VPC has both legacy VPC firewall rules and an associated global network firewall policy, and the network's firewall policy enforcement order is at its default setting. An organization-level hierarchical policy uses `goto_next` for all traffic. In which order are rules evaluated for a VM in that VPC?
Global network firewall policy, then VPC firewall rules, then hierarchical policy.
VPC firewall rules, then hierarchical policy, then global network firewall policy.
Hierarchical policy, then global network firewall policy, then VPC firewall rules.
Hierarchical policy, then VPC firewall rules, then global network firewall policy.

Hierarchical policies are always evaluated first, and with the default enforcement order (`AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL`), VPC firewall rules are evaluated before the global network firewall policy, followed by any regional network firewall policy.
The order between VPC rules and network policies can be switched with the enforcement-order setting.

An auditor asks for logs of all denied inbound connection attempts to VMs in a VPC. Firewall Rules Logging is enabled on every custom rule, but denied connections that don't match any custom rule aren't logged. What should the engineer do?
Enable logging on the implied deny ingress rule.
Create an explicit deny-all ingress rule with a priority just above the implied rule (for example, 65534) and enable logging on it.
Enable VPC Flow Logs with a sampling rate of 1.0.
Enable Packet Mirroring for all VMs.
Implied rules can't have logging enabled, so an explicit, logged deny-all rule at a low priority captures traffic that would otherwise hit the implied deny.
VPC Flow Logs record accepted flows rather than firewall deny decisions, and Packet Mirroring is costly and doesn't record firewall actions.

A PCI workload's VMs must not send traffic to the internet, but they must reach internal services in `10.0.0.0/8` and Google APIs via `private.googleapis.com`. The engineer wants a firewall-based control. Which set of egress rules meets the requirement?
Deny egress `0.0.0.0/0` at priority 65000; allow egress to `10.0.0.0/8` and `199.36.153.8/30` at priority 1000.
Allow egress to `10.0.0.0/8` at priority 65000; deny egress `0.0.0.0/0` at priority 1000.
Deny egress `0.0.0.0/0` at priority 1000; allow egress to `10.0.0.0/8` and `199.36.153.8/30` at priority 65000.
Rely on the implied egress deny rule and add allow rules for `10.0.0.0/8` only.
Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so the specific allow rules at priority 1000 permit internal and API traffic before the broad deny at 65000 blocks everything else.
Options B and C place the deny ahead of the allows, blocking required traffic, and the implied egress rule is allow, not deny.

A VPC has an ingress rule allowing TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` to web servers and an egress rule denying all traffic from those servers. Clients initiate HTTPS connections to the web servers. What happens?
Connections fail because the egress deny blocks responses.
Connections succeed only if an egress allow rule for ephemeral ports is added.
Connections succeed because firewall rules are stateful and return traffic for allowed connections is permitted.
Connections succeed only for IPv6 clients.
Google Cloud firewall rules are stateful, so once an ingress connection is allowed, response traffic is permitted regardless of egress rules.
Ephemeral-port egress rules are needed with stateless ACLs, not with VPC firewalls, and IP version doesn't change stateful behavior.
A company wants to move 400 VPC firewall rules into a global network firewall policy to use secure tags and FQDN objects, with minimal risk of accidental exposure. What's the recommended approach?
Delete the VPC firewall rules and recreate them manually in the policy.

Use the firewall migration tooling (`gcloud compute network-firewall-policies migrate`) to generate the policy, review it, associate it with the VPC, validate behavior, and then change the enforcement order and remove the legacy rules.
Create a hierarchical firewall policy with the same rules at the organization level.
Disable all VPC firewall rules and rely on Cloud Armor.

Google provides a migration tool that converts VPC firewall rules into a network firewall policy, letting teams review and validate before cutting over via the enforcement order and removing legacy rules.
Manual recreation is error-prone, moving VPC-specific rules to the organization level changes their scope, and Cloud Armor protects load balancers rather than VM-level east-west traffic.

A security team maintains a list of 60 partner IP ranges that must be allowed in rules across multiple firewall policies. The list changes monthly, and updates currently require editing many rules. What should the engineer use?
Network tags on every partner-facing VM.
A Cloud Armor security policy with the ranges.
A single firewall rule per partner range.
An address group referenced by the firewall policy rules.
Address groups are reusable collections of IP ranges that can be referenced in firewall policy rules, so one update propagates to every rule that uses the group.
Network tags identify targets rather than external sources, Cloud Armor only applies at load balancers, and one rule per range increases management overhead.

A company has VMs with external IP addresses that aren't behind a load balancer. The security team wants to block inbound connections from specific countries and from known malicious IP addresses maintained by Google, without maintaining IP lists themselves. What should the engineer configure?
Network firewall policy rules that use geolocation objects and Google Threat Intelligence lists as sources.
Cloud Armor security policies attached to the VMs.
VPC firewall rules with manually maintained country IP ranges.
Cloud NAT rules that drop traffic by source country.
Cloud NGFW firewall policies support geolocation objects and Google-managed Threat Intelligence lists, which are updated automatically.
Cloud Armor attaches to load balancer backends rather than standalone VMs, manually maintained lists are error-prone, and Cloud NAT handles outbound translation rather than inbound filtering.

A company deployed Cloud NGFW Enterprise with an intrusion prevention security profile. Test attacks sent over plain HTTP are detected and blocked, but the same attacks sent over HTTPS pass through undetected. What should the engineer do?
Increase the threat severity level in the security profile to "critical."
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on the rules that apply the security profile group.
Configure TLS inspection with a Certificate Authority Service CA pool and a TLS inspection policy, enable it on the rules, and distribute the CA certificate to clients.
Replace the firewall endpoint with Cloud Armor.

Encrypted payloads can't be inspected until Cloud NGFW Enterprise decrypts them with TLS inspection, which uses Certificate Authority Service and requires clients to trust the issuing CA. Severity settings and logging don't provide decryption, and Cloud Armor protects load balancers rather than inspecting VM traffic.

A company enabled Cloud NGFW Enterprise intrusion prevention for a VPC. VMs in `us-central1-a` are protected, but VMs in `us-central1-b` and `us-central1-c` aren't being inspected, even though the firewall policy rule with `apply_security_profile_group` targets all VMs. What's the cause?
Security profiles only apply to the first zone in a region.
The firewall policy must be regional rather than global.
The rule's priority is lower than the implied allow egress rule.
Firewall endpoints are zonal, so an endpoint and a VPC association are needed in each zone where workloads run.

Cloud NGFW Enterprise firewall endpoints are zonal resources, and traffic is only inspected in zones where an endpoint exists and is associated with the VPC. Security profiles apply in all zones with endpoints, both global and regional policies can reference profiles, and implied rules have the lowest priority.

A regional internal Application Load Balancer fronts VMs. Health checks pass, but client requests forwarded by the load balancer are rejected at the backends. Firewall rules allow health check ranges and client subnets. What additional ingress rule is required?
Allow ingress from the proxy-only subnet range to the backends on the serving ports.
Allow ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` on the serving ports.
Allow ingress from the load balancer's forwarding rule IP address.
Envoy proxies for internal Application Load Balancers connect to backends from the proxy-only subnet, so backends must allow ingress from that range.
The IAP range is for TCP forwarding, opening to the internet violates least privilege, and the forwarding rule IP isn't the source of proxied connections.

A media company is consolidating two websites behind one global external Application Load Balancer. Requests to `www.example.com/api/*` must go to a GKE service exposed through zonal NEGs, requests to `www.example.com/static/*` must be served from a Cloud Storage bucket, and all requests to `shop.example.com` must go to a Compute Engine managed instance group. How should the engineer configure the load balancer?
Create three forwarding rules with different IP addresses, one per backend.

Create a URL map with host rules for `www.example.com` and `shop.example.com`; the `www` path matcher routes `/api/*` to a backend service with the NEGs and `/static/*` to a backend bucket, and the `shop` path matcher defaults to the MIG backend service.
Create a single backend service containing the NEGs, the bucket, and the MIG, and use balancing modes to separate traffic.
Use Cloud DNS routing policies to send each path to a different load balancer.

URL maps use host rules and path matchers to route by hostname and path to different backend services and backend buckets behind a single IP. Separate forwarding rules aren't necessary, a backend service can't contain a Cloud Storage bucket or mix these backend types for path routing, and DNS can't route by URL path.

A global external Application Load Balancer has a backend service with managed instance groups in `us-east1` and `us-west1`. The team must perform maintenance on the `us-east1` MIG and wants new requests to shift to `us-west1` without deleting the backend or changing the MIG size. What should the engineer do?
Delete the health check so the backend is marked unhealthy.
Change the balancing mode of the `us-east1` backend to `CONNECTION`.
Remove the `us-east1` firewall rule for health check ranges.
Set the capacity scaler of the `us-east1` backend to 0.
Setting a backend's capacity scaler to 0 stops the load balancer from sending it new requests while keeping the backend configured, which is the intended way to drain it.
Deleting the health check or blocking health check traffic forces failures instead of a controlled drain, and changing the balancing mode doesn't remove capacity.

A B2B web application behind a global external Application Load Balancer uses client IP session affinity to keep users on the same backend. Customers report that almost all traffic from a large enterprise customer lands on a single overloaded VM. That customer's users reach the internet through a few corporate NAT addresses. What should the engineer change?
Switch session affinity to generated cookie affinity.
Switch session affinity to none and store sessions on local disk.
Increase the maximum requests per second for the overloaded VM.
Client IP affinity maps all users behind the same NAT address to the same backend, while generated cookie affinity keys on a per-client cookie set by the load balancer and spreads users evenly.
Removing affinity breaks sessions stored locally, and changing capacity or balancing mode doesn't change affinity-based concentration.

A company deploys the same Cloud Run service in `us-central1`, `europe-west1`, and `asia-east1`. It wants a single global IP, a custom domain with a managed certificate, Cloud Armor protection, and routing to the nearest region. What should the engineer configure?
A regional external Application Load Balancer in each region with an internet NEG pointing to the Cloud Run URL.
Cloud Run domain mapping in each region and Cloud DNS geolocation routing.
A global external Application Load Balancer with a backend service containing one serverless NEG per region.
An external passthrough Network Load Balancer with Cloud Run as a backend.

Serverless NEGs are regional, so a global external Application Load Balancer backend service with one serverless NEG per region provides a single anycast IP, proximity routing, managed certificates, and Cloud Armor.
Regional load balancers or domain mappings don't give a single global entry point with Cloud Armor, and passthrough Network Load Balancers don't support serverless backends.
